p1.title: Passage 1
paras: How can we tell a scientific theory from a merely confident opinion? One influential answer is that a scientific theory must take a risk. It must forbid certain things from happening, so that if those things are observed, the theory is shown to be false. The claim that all metals expand when heated is scientific in this sense: a single metal that contracted under heat would refute it. By contrast, a theory that can explain every possible outcome, whatever happens, has not thereby proved its strength. It has revealed that it says nothing definite about the world.

This criterion, usually called falsifiability, has a curious consequence. No number of confirming observations can establish a general theory beyond doubt, since the next observation might be the exception; yet one well-founded contrary observation can overturn it. Science, on this view, advances not by piling up proofs but by surviving attempts at refutation. Critics have pointed out that working scientists rarely abandon a theory at the first awkward result. They suspect their instruments, adjust auxiliary assumptions and wait for the anomaly to be explained, and sometimes they are right to do so. Even so, the central insight endures. A theory earns our trust not by being impossible to challenge but by having been exposed to challenge and having, so far, withstood it.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Discussions of urban transport tend to revolve around metro rail lines and flyovers, projects that are visible, expensive and politically rewarding to inaugurate. The humble bus receives far less attention, although in most Indian cities it carries more passengers than any other form of public transport. A bus route requires no tunnelling and can be redrawn within weeks as a city grows. A single bus occupies the road space of two or three cars while carrying many times as many people. Its weakness is not the vehicle but the conditions in which it must operate: buses stuck in the same traffic as private cars lose their advantage of speed, and passengers who wait forty minutes at an unsheltered stop soon conclude that a two-wheeler is the only sensible choice.

The remedies are well known and modest in cost. Dedicated lanes at congested junctions, frequent and reliable services, shelters with accurate arrival information and fares integrated with other modes would transform the bus from a last resort into a first choice. That such measures are so rarely implemented says less about their merit than about who uses buses. Their passengers are disproportionately students, women, the elderly and workers on low wages, groups whose daily inconvenience seldom reaches the desks where budgets are decided.

opts: The idea that a scientific theory must be open to refutation and earns trust by surviving tests.
The impossibility of any scientific knowledge.
The physical properties of heated metals.
questions.why: Main idea: falsifiability; 'A theory earns our trust... by having been exposed to challenge and having, so far, withstood it'.

questions.q: Which example does the passage give of a scientific claim?
opts: Every possible outcome can be explained.
questions.why: Detail: 'The claim that all metals expand when heated is scientific in this sense'.

questions.q: The author would regard a theory that can explain every possible outcome as:
opts: The strongest kind of scientific theory.
Lacking definite content, rather than being especially strong.
questions.why: Inference: such a theory 'has not thereby proved its strength. It has revealed that it says nothing definite'.

questions.q: The critics mentioned in the passage point out that:
opts: In practice, scientists rarely discard a theory at the first contrary result.
Confirming observations can prove a theory beyond doubt.
questions.why: Detail: 'working scientists rarely abandon a theory at the first awkward result'.

questions.q: The word "auxiliary" in "adjust auxiliary assumptions" most nearly means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: scientists adjust the subsidiary assumptions around a theory rather than its core.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Why Metro Rail Is the Only Solution
The Neglected Bus: An Efficient Answer Overlooked
questions.why: Main idea: the bus 'receives far less attention' though it carries the most passengers and could become 'a first choice' with modest measures.

questions.q: According to the passage, one advantage of a bus route is that it:
opts: is never affected by traffic congestion.
is more rewarding for politicians to inaugurate.
can be redrawn within weeks as a city grows.
questions.why: Detail: 'A bus route requires no tunnelling and can be redrawn within weeks as a city grows.'

questions.q: The final sentence of the passage implies that improvements to buses are neglected partly because:
opts: bus passengers do not want better services.
their users have little influence over budget decisions.
no one knows what measures would help.
questions.why: Inference: users' 'daily inconvenience seldom reaches the desks where budgets are decided'; the author says the remedies 'are well known and modest in cost'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards metro lines and flyovers is:
opts: mildly critical of the attention they receive at the expense of buses.
strongly opposed to their construction in any city.
questions.why: Tone: they are described as 'politically rewarding to inaugurate' while the bus 'receives far less attention'; the author does not call for stopping them.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'humble' most nearly means:
opts: ordinary and modest, attracting little notice
questions.why: Vocabulary: the 'humble bus' is contrasted with 'visible, expensive' metro and flyover projects.
